posts.title: Casting light: notes from the Shimogamo pour
posts.excerpt: 38 cubic metres in one continuous lift, so that no cold joint would cross the light. A morning on site at the reading room.
posts.content:
At 05:40 on the twelfth of September the first truck turned into Shimogamo-Hon-dori. By noon the north wall of the reading room was full: 38 cubic metres of concrete, poured in one continuous lift so that no cold joint would cross the light.

The wall is 7.2 metres tall and 21 metres long. It carries almost nothing — the roof rests on four steel columns set back from its face — but it does the most important work in the building. It is the surface the skylight was drawn for. For eleven months a day, it is what readers will look at when they lift their eyes from the page.

Formwork chosen board by board

We used Japanese cedar boards, 120 millimetres wide, sandblasted to raise the grain and laid with the growth rings alternating, so that the imprint reads as texture rather than pattern. Every board was selected at the yard in Kitayama by our project architect, Sae Nakamura, and her carpenter, Mr Iwata, who has built formwork for us since 2012.

A wall like this is drawn in a week and cast in a morning. Then it takes ten years to become what we drew.

Aiko Morishita, partner

What we measured

  • Slump 18 cm, water–cement ratio 0.45, fly ash 15 %
  • Pour rate 1.2 m per hour, vibrated in 40 cm layers
  • Formwork struck after nine days; wall cured under wet hessian for three weeks

The reading room opens to the neighbourhood in April 2027. Until then, the wall will stand behind scaffolding, slowly losing its new grey to the colour of the river stones in the Kamo.
